transcript: okay I wanna defend jukebox musicals from like an intellectual artsy perspective and I specify that because I feel like the more broad defenses already exist right like “they're popular for a reason” “just let people people enjoy them” “they're a good gateway for people into theatre” but like if you're a theatre snob then those defenses probably don't mean much to you so like let’s intellectualise it a little bit shall we? of course we know that jukebox musicals are a sub art form of musical theatre and the musical theatre purists don't like them because of this like Sondheimian ethos of specificity: that the music and lyrics have to be completely molded to suit the storytelling needs of the book and that was true and brilliant for the type of work that Sondheim was doing and he was the best at doing it but if we just zoom out for a second Theatr is a very broad art form and there's lots of different ways to use and adapt existing text and what's interesting is that in the world of like downtown experimental plays and stuff like that the use of pre existing text is considered a totally viable and well respected art form we have verbatim theatre or documentary theatre people using transcripts from interviews FBl investigations court trials, TV broadcast old letters, emails, whatever and here's the point right? no one is out here saying that those theater makers are lazy for not writing their own scripts or that like it shouldn't count as theatre and personally I find this kind of theatre fascinating and exciting to be like okay this existed in real life outside the world of the play and now, how are we seeing it differently? what perspective and we gain on it by seeing it in either a different context or a more distilled curated context? and in theory at least you could apply all of this same logic to jukebox musicals where some people would say that putting a pre existing song in a new narrative context creates an incongruity I would say that if done right it would create more of like a conversation a kind of tension between the old and the new between one context and another that would allow you to see both of them in a new and more interesting light and with jukebox musicals there's also the added layer of not only the songs themselves being pre existing but the audience's emotional relationship to those songs and again while some people might say that it's like “cheating” to capitalize on nostalgia for storytelling purposes I would say it's fair game and when done well you can tap into something very deep and powerful but here's the twist right? I also don't like the majority of jukebox musicals I've hated more jukebox musicals than I can count but I don't think it's because they're jukebox musicals I think it's a correlation, not a causation I'm often frustrated by them when they are boring and formulaic and they don't seem to care about making something creative they just want to crank out a product to make a quick buck but that's not unique to jukebox musicals you know how many original musicals I've seen how many original plays I've seen that were not only super lazily written but painfully glaringly derivative and I think a lot of the anger against jukebox musicals as a concept as an artistic form would be better directed at just general artistic laziness on a reliance on stale formulas and rushed development processes and theatre ecosystems that are fettered to capitalism
